extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, managers, evaluators, and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and measures for designing and conducting evaluation research in public relations, including survey question types, content analysis, readability measures, techniques for measuring communication/retention/attitudes/behaviors, and scoring formulas for cognitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time budgets (three calculation methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time budgets can be used as an internal management control technique to examine how people on a public relations staff allocate their time in different forms of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three ways to calculate time budgets: (1) Each person maintains a diary on an hourly basis during a specified period (most extensive but may change behavior because of recording). (2) Interview people the day after about previous day’s activity and enter results on an interview schedule. (3) Random-time sampling: subjects are told to record what they are doing at randomly selected times announced by one person who knows the times; over a week or longer the random times give an accurate picture for groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between open- and closed-end questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to use open-end or closed-end questions in survey instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closed-end questions whenever you can because they are easier for respondents and easier to analyze. Use open-end questions for qualitative research, exploratory/formative evaluations, and as probes to get more detail about an opinion measured on a closed-end question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact (demographic) questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions that collect demographic/factual information about respondents (sex, age, income, number of TV sets, newspapers read).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write as multiple-choice items. Generally provide five response choices (although some researchers prefer more or fewer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative questions (measuring beliefs and attitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions that place respondents on a numerical scale from low to high to measure beliefs and attitudes; ideally use several measures of the same attitude and sum into a single scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four major forms: (a) multiple-choice rating items (Excellent/Good/Average/Poor/Very poor), (b) Likert-type agreement/disagreement with five response choices including a neutral point, (c) semantic differential technique using polar adjectives on a seven-point scale, and (d) rankings (respondents rank items relative to each other). Use several items and sum them to form scales when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask respondents how much they know, what they know, how they learned about something, or when they heard about something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally write as multiple-choice questions to measure knowledge and message exposure/retention; used frequently in readership studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-perception questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions asking respondents’ opinions about facts or about their own behavior (respondent-provided perceptions which may or may not be accurate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to measure problem recognition, involvement, constraint recognition, referent criterion, information processing, and similar constructs; write as multiple-choice frequency or category items where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring the Communication objective (counts and indirect indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: When objectives are defined as communication, measure evidence that messages have moved to and been received by target publics or management subsystems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect measures and counts include: number of press clippings appearing in the media (note: clippings do not guarantee readership), number of contacts with journalists, TV/radio ratings from rating companies, attendance counts at exhibits/open houses/special events, number of speeches given by employees, number of people exposed to educational materials, number of publications distributed to each public, number of organizational managers briefed, number of dialogue sessions between managers and publics (symmetric communication), readership studies, and content analysis of clippings/publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of messages — general approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Four ways to measure whether publics or organizational subsystems have retained a message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches include: (1) Readability formulas as indicators of comprehension difficulty (indirect measure of retention), (2) the Signaled Stopping Technique (SST) to observe processing while reading/listening, (3) multiple-choice comprehension questions where the correct message is one of several plausible alternatives, and (4) other direct comprehension/recall measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readership surveys (measuring who read/seen messages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys that document whether clippings were read, whether employees read a publication, or whether anyone saw a TV ad/program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be done by personal interview, telephone, or mail. In person, show the publication/article and ask recall and how much was read (read all/most/some/not at all). Telephone/mail require describing the story or reading the title before asking recall; can ask frequency scales for whole publications or types of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content analysis (systematic measurement of message content)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic, quantitative method of determining the content of mass media, clippings, organizational publications, speeches, or other messages to quantify themes, valence, and topic distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five major stages: (1) select a unit of analysis (article/paragraph/sentence), (2) construct categories defined by what the PR program was designed to communicate, (3) sample content (randomly or by time period), (4) code units of analysis (train coders and check coder reliability), and (5) analyze results by computer or hand. Check coder reliability: if coders disagree more than about 10–20% of the time, reconstruct categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability formulas (measuring text difficulty as proxy for retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative formulas that indicate whether written materials are appropriate for audiences with different educational backgrounds; predict readability/listenability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common formulas measure word difficulty and sentence length (Flesch Reading Ease, Gunning Fog Index, Farr-Jenkins-Patterson, Dale-Chall). Use a 100-word continuous sample (preferably not at the beginning). For Flesch, compute average sentence length and syllables per 100 words and apply R = (.0778)(ASL) + (.0455)(syllables/100 words) — 2.209; interpret score bands (e.g., 4.0–4.5 very easy through 7.5+ academic). For Gunning Fog, count average sentence length and polysyllables (with exceptions) and multiply sum by 0.4 to estimate years of education required; keep writing below danger line (score of 13). Use readability formulas only as general indicators of difficulty and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signaled Stopping Technique (SST)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique (developed by Richard Carter) that lets evaluators see what happens in readers’ minds as they read a message, to determine if readers process the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give subjects the message and ask them to put a slash where they feel like stopping and mark reason codes: C = confusion, R = to reread, ? = to ask a question, T = to think about the idea, U = because you understand, A = to agree, D = to disagree, or write other reasons. Analyze stop points and reasons to identify comprehension problems and opportunities to improve writing. SST can also be used for spoken messages (subjects write codes as they listen), though it is harder to map reactions to specific parts of spoken material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-choice comprehension questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehension items in which the organization’s correct message is one of several reasonable-sounding alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a plausible 'don't know' option. Use as a direct measure of message retention; construct distractors that sound reasonable so the correct message stands out only to those who retained it (example: which statement represents company position).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of cognitions (measuring agreement with organizational beliefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether respondents agree with the company’s position (acceptance of cognitions) using evaluative follow-up questions after comprehension items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask Likert-type questions about agreement with statements representing organizational and antiorganization beliefs. Prepare at least two statements (one for organization belief, one for opposing belief) that are not exact opposites so respondents may agree with both. Use responses to measure hedging and wedging; follow-up evaluations can be mixed with other belief items to avoid immediate adjacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring wedge (quantitative formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quantitative measure of wedging—extent to which a respondent believes one statement but not the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute Wedge = ABS(Question 1 — Question 2) using numerical Likert scores; take absolute value so sign is ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring hedge (quantitative formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quantitative measure of hedging—extent to which a respondent believes both conflicting statements to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute Hedge = Question 1 + Question 2 — ABS(Question 1 — Question 2). This reduces false high hedging scores that can arise when one response is extreme and the other is opposite. Note: respondents who choose a 'no opinion' option cannot be scored for hedging/wedging on those items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative measures of cognitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use open-end questions or informal methods to ask people whether they believe the company’s position, critics’ positions, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask respondents to talk about the issue and introduce factual statements; analyze statements to determine which alleged facts respondents accept. Use when you want richer, exploratory data beyond closed-end measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientational measure of understanding (difference score)
rubrics_metrics.description: A symmetric measure of overlapping cognitions (understanding) between an organization and a public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate a difference score by subtracting the average score of management (or other group) from the average score of the public and taking the absolute value. Higher difference = lower understanding. Example: avg_management 4.5 vs avg_public 2.2 gives difference 2.3 on 1–5 scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude measurement (evaluation/behavioral intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure attitudes (evaluations or behavioral intentions) using evaluative Likert-type questions similar to cognition measures but asking how strongly respondents believe solutions or behaviors should be chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple evaluative items, open-end questions for suggestions about actions, and coorientational difference scores to produce symmetric measures of agreement between groups (compute differences between average evaluative scores for groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overt behavior measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure actual respondent behaviors taken to influence or resolve an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closed-end questions asking whether respondents engaged in specified behaviors (with an open 'other' option), open-end/informal questions, informal or formal observation of behaviors, and actual counts (telephone calls, letters, funds raised, attendance). Example closed items: written letters to NRC, written to senator, refused to travel near plant. Note that combination of methods and sequencing (open + closed) can measure multiple objectives in order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination and sequencing of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine open- and closed-end questions and other methods to measure several objectives in sequence during an evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ask membership and conversation recall (closed), then ask what was learned (open), then ask evaluative judgment (closed choice: good/bad/no effect), then ask whether respondent acted and what they did (open/closed). Use sequencing to trace exposure → comprehension → acceptance → behavior.
